title: The Longest Age
subtitle: What the Stone Age is, why the name misleads, and how we can know anything about it
summary: The oldest tools, the museum keeper who named the age, the clocks, molecules and ice that let us read three million years, the ice ages and the arguments about what ended them, and the whole story in one sweep.
statusNote: First full draft of episode 1, for feedback on voices, tone, pacing and the handling of contested views before the other episodes are written.

sites.name: La Pasiega
sites.summary: A cave in Cantabria where a red ladder-shaped sign lies under a calcite crust dated by uranium-thorium to at least 64,800 years, one of three Spanish caves that Hoffmann and colleagues (2018) attributed to Neanderthal painters. The dates are contested.

sites.name: Maltravieso
sites.summary: A cave in Extremadura with dozens of hand stencils; a crust over one stencil gave a minimum uranium-thorium age of about 66,700 years in the 2018 study, which critics argue may reflect uranium loss rather than true age.

sites.name: Cueva de Ardales
sites.summary: A cave near Málaga where red pigment on stalagmite curtains was dated by crusts to at least 65,500 years; later work argued that the pigment was applied deliberately in several episodes over tens of thousands of years.

sites.name: Kap København
sites.summary: Frozen sediments at the northern tip of Greenland yielded the oldest DNA yet read, from a two-million-year-old forest with mastodons, reindeer and hares (Kjær and colleagues, 2022).

sites.name: Little Dome C
sites.dateLabel: ice more than 1.2 million years old
sites.summary: Drilling site of the Beyond EPICA project, where a 2,800-metre ice core reached bedrock in January 2025 with a continuous climate record of more than 1.2 million years.

sites.name: Murray Springs
sites.summary: A Clovis site in Arizona where a dark organic layer, the black mat, lies over the last mammoth bones; a key site for both sides of the Younger Dryas impact debate.

sites.name: Saint-Acheul, Amiens
sites.summary: The gravel pits of the Somme terraces at Amiens, where handaxes lay among the bones of extinct elephants and rhinoceroses. Joseph Prestwich and John Evans watched one being dug from undisturbed gravel here in April 1859, and the Acheulean takes its name from the place.

sites.name: Brixham Cave (Windmill Hill Cavern)
sites.summary: A cave discovered by quarrying in January 1858 and excavated under William Pengelly for the Geological and Royal Societies: flint tools sealed beneath a stalagmite floor among the bones of cave bear, rhinoceros and mammoth, the first widely accepted proof that people had lived alongside extinct animals.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: On the morning of the ninth of July 2011, a team of archaeologists took a wrong turn.

shots.caption: The eastern shore of Lake Turkana, Kenya

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: They were looking for a fossil site west of Lake Turkana, in northern Kenya, and found instead a hillside scattered with broken stones. Sonia Harmand and Jason Lewis of Stony Brook University named the place Lomekwi 3.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Someone had struck these stones from lava cobbles 3.3 million years ago. The layer that held them lies above a volcanic ash dated to 3.32 million years, and the magnetic record in the sediment agrees. If that reading holds, they are the oldest known tools made by breaking stone, 700,000 years older than any found before.

shots.caption: Kenyanthropus platyops, found at Lomekwi in 1999, about 3.5 million years old

params.title: Lomekwi 3, West Turkana
params.surface: Surface finds: 130 or so pieces on the slope

shots.label: The oldest known knapped stone, if the context holds

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: From that moment until metal arrived, only 5,000 to 7,000 years ago in the places that had it first, our ancestors and their relatives lived in what we call the Stone Age. It covers more than 99 percent of the human technological past.

shots.label: of the time since the first known tools falls within the Stone Age
shots.kicker: 3.3 million years of stone, about 5,000 of metal

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: This is the story of that age, on every continent, from the first flaked stones to the first furnaces.

shots.title: The Longest Age
shots.sub: A world history of the Stone Age

sources.cite: Harmand, S. et al. (2015). 3.3-million-year-old stone tools from Lomekwi 3, West Turkana, Kenya. Nature 521, 310–315.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The name was born in a museum. In 1816 Christian Jürgensen Thomsen, a Copenhagen merchant’s son and a self-taught antiquarian, took charge of Denmark’s collection of antiquities. He sorted its cutting tools by material, and noticed which objects turned up together in graves and hoards: first stone, then bronze, then iron. His guidebook of 1836 put the three ages into print.

card.title: Christian Jürgensen Thomsen
items: Age of Stone
Age of Bronze
Age of Iron
card.note: Ledetraad til Nordisk Oldkyndighed, 1836; English edition 1848

cues.speaker: source
cues.text: The Age of Stone, or that period when weapons and implements were made of stone, wood, bone, or some such material, and during which very little or nothing at all was known of metals.

card.text: The Age of Stone, or that period when weapons and implements were made of stone, wood, bone, or some such material, and during which very little or nothing at all was known of metals.
card.attribution: Guide to Northern Archaeology, London, 1848, translated from Thomsen’s Danish guidebook of 1836

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Thirty years later the English banker and naturalist John Lubbock split the stone part in two, in a book he called Pre-historic Times.

cues.speaker: source
cues.text: First, that of the Drift; when man shared the possession of Europe with the Mammoth, the Cave bear, the Woolly-haired rhinoceros, and other extinct animals. This we may call the Palaeolithic period.

card.text: First, that of the Drift; when man shared the possession of Europe with the Mammoth, the Cave bear, the Woolly-haired rhinoceros, and other extinct animals.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Lubbock’s Palaeolithic and Neolithic, the old and the new stone ages, are still the words we use. In 1929 John Goodwin and Clarence van Riet Lowe, finding the European terms a poor fit for southern Africa, divided the African record into an Earlier, Middle and Later Stone Age instead. Every region now has its own sequence. But the label misleads. Stone is simply what survives.

card.title: Regional sequences
items: Europe and West Asia: Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic, then Mesolithic and Neolithic
Africa: Earlier, Middle and Later Stone Age (Goodwin and van Riet Lowe, 1929)
Japan: Jōmon, the age of cord-marked pottery
The Americas: Paleoindian and Archaic

Lubbock, J. (1865). Pre-historic Times, as Illustrated by Ancient Remains, and the Manners and Customs of Modern Savages. London: Williams and Norgate.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Thomsen’s ages had no dates. In his day the accepted age of humanity was a few thousand years, and the idea that people had lived alongside mammoths was close to heresy. The discovery that the Stone Age was deep took two decades of argument, and it is where this series’ habit of naming who argued what begins.

shots.caption: Thomsen showing visitors around the museum in Copenhagen, drawing of 1848

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: In the 1830s and 1840s Jacques Boucher de Perthes, a customs officer at Abbeville in northern France, collected flint handaxes from the gravel pits of the Somme, where they lay among the bones of extinct elephants and rhinoceroses. His book, printed in 1847, argued that people had made the tools before the biblical flood. The learned societies of Paris ignored it, and the customs officer’s belief that other flints were carved figures of animals and people did not help his case.

shots.caption: A flint handaxe from Menchecourt near Abbeville, from Boucher de Perthes’ collection

captions: Handaxes from the Moulin Quignon pit at Abbeville

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The test came from England. In January 1858 quarrying at Brixham in Devon broke into a cave, and the Geological Society organised an excavation under the schoolteacher William Pengelly. Beneath an unbroken floor of stalagmite lay the bones of cave bear, rhinoceros and mammoth, and among them flint tools. In April 1859 the geologist Joseph Prestwich and the paper manufacturer and antiquarian John Evans crossed to Abbeville and Amiens to see the gravels for themselves. At Saint-Acheul they watched a handaxe being dug out of undisturbed gravel more than five metres down, and had it photographed in place.

shots.caption: The entrance to Windmill Hill Cavern, Brixham, Devon
Section through Brixham Cave, from John Evans, The Ancient Stone Implements, 1872
Windmill Hill Cavern as a show cave, before 1906

captions: John Evans, paper manufacturer and antiquarian

shots.caption: Handaxes from the Saint-Acheul gravels, Amiens

cues.speaker: source
cues.text: Lying in the gravel at a depth of 17 feet from the original surface, and six and a half feet from the chalk.

shots.kicker: Joseph Prestwich, read to the Royal Society, 26 May 1859
shots.text: Lying in the gravel at a depth of 17 feet from the original surface, and six and a half feet from the chalk.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Prestwich read the results to the Royal Society on the 26th of May 1859, and Evans to the Society of Antiquaries a week later. That November Darwin published On the Origin of Species, and in 1863 Charles Lyell’s Geological Evidences of the Antiquity of Man gathered the case. Within five years the human past had grown from a few thousand years to an unmeasured depth. It would take another century, and the clocks you will hear about shortly, to put numbers on it.

params.title: Five years that deepened the past

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Even the beginning of the age is argued over. Lomekwi 3 is a single site, and a claim this old draws hard questions. Throughout this series, each side will be stated as its supporters put it.

cues.speaker: research
cues.text: Sonia Harmand, Jason Lewis and their colleagues, writing in Nature in 2015, describe 149 artefacts, about twenty of them excavated from undisturbed sediment. The cores and flakes carry the scars that repeated, deliberate striking produces, and several flakes fit back onto their cores.

card.question: Are the Lomekwi 3 stones the oldest tools?

views.label: Yes, 3.3 million years
views.text: Harmand, Lewis and colleagues (2015): artefacts excavated in place, knapping scars and refits, a layer above an ash dated to 3.32 million years, and a matching magnetic record.

views.label: Not yet shown
views.text: Domínguez-Rodrigo and Alcalá (2016, 2019): most pieces were surface finds, the excavated sample is small, and natural breakage can imitate knapping. Archer, Aldeias and McPherron (2020): the paper stretched the meaning of in situ.

card.status: Widely cited as the oldest evidence of knapping, but still one site. A second site of similar age, or new excavation at Lomekwi, would settle it.

cues.speaker: research
cues.text: Manuel Domínguez-Rodrigo and Luis Alcalá, in 2016 and again in 2019, answer that most of the pieces lay on the surface, where they could have arrived from younger layers, and that natural processes can break stone in ways that imitate knapping. In 2020 Will Archer, Vera Aldeias and Shannon McPherron argued that the original paper had stretched the meaning of the words in situ. Harmand and her colleagues replied that the excavated pieces came from an intact layer, and that the surface finds share the same raw materials and the same style.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Where does the field stand? The 3.3-million-year date is widely cited, and no second site that old has been found. The continuous record of flaked tools begins between 3 and 2.6 million years ago, at Nyayanga in Kenya and at Ledi-Geraru and Gona in Ethiopia.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Either way, the Stone Age did not begin with one invention, but with a slow change in how our relatives used stone. We will return to Lomekwi in the next episode. First, a question this whole series depends on: how can we know any of this?

card.title: How we know
items: Clocks in volcanic ash, cave crystals and sand
DNA from bones and cave dirt
Proteins from teeth two million years old
Ice and ocean mud that remember the climate

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Stone dominates museum cases for one reason: it survives. Almost everything else rots. Where conditions are exceptional, glimpses of the rest appear.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: In an open-cast coal mine at Schöningen, in northern Germany, excavators in the 1990s found wooden spears up to two and a half metres long, lying among the bones of some fifty butchered horses. Lakeshore mud had sealed them from oxygen. For years the spears were dated to about 300,000 years. In 2025 a team led by Jarod Hutson, with dating by Kirsty Penkman’s laboratory in York, measured the slow chemical change of amino acids sealed inside snail shells from the same layer and put the horizon at about 200,000 years, which would make the hunters Neanderthals rather than their ancestors.

cues.speaker: research
cues.text: The two dates rest on different evidence. The older figure came from the sequence of glacial deposits above and below the finds; the newer one from amino acids, whose rate of change depends on the temperatures the shells experienced over thousands of years. The two lines of evidence do not yet agree, and both dates appear in the literature.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: String is another example. In 2020 Bruce Hardy and colleagues reported a fragment of three-ply cord, twisted from the inner bark of a conifer, stuck to a stone tool at Abri du Maras in southern France and made by Neanderthals roughly 50,000 years ago. In 2024 Nicholas Conard and Veerle Rots showed that a baton of mammoth ivory from Hohle Fels in southwest Germany, about 37,000 years old and pierced by four spirally grooved holes, was most likely a tool for making rope. With replicas, experimenters twisted cattail fibres into metres of strong cord in minutes.

card.title: What cord implies
items: Nets, snares and fishing lines
Bags, baskets and slings
Lashings for hafted tools and shelters
Almost none of it survives

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: At Kalambo Falls in Zambia, two logs notched to fit together, at least 476,000 years old, were preserved by waterlogging and published in 2023 by Larry Barham and colleagues. Every such find is a reminder that the Stone Age toolkit was mostly not stone, and that the record we have is a record of what lasts.

sources.cite: Hutson, J. M. et al. (2025). Revised age for Schöningen hunting spears indicates intensification of Neanderthal cooperative behavior around 200,000 years ago. Science Advances 11, eadv0752.
Hardy, B. L. et al. (2020). Direct evidence of Neanderthal fibre technology and its cognitive and behavioral implications. Scientific Reports 10, 4889.
Conard, N. J. & Rots, V. (2024). Rope making in the Aurignacian of Central Europe more than 35,000 years ago. Science Advances 10, eadh5217.
Barham, L. et al. (2023). Evidence for the earliest structural use of wood at least 476,000 years ago. Nature 622, 107–111.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Before the clocks, a word about ground. Archaeology reads layers. Sediment settles in order, oldest at the bottom, and an object sealed in an undisturbed layer belongs to the time of that layer. Most arguments about early sites, Lomekwi included, are arguments about whether a layer really was undisturbed, and whether the objects in it are what they seem.

layers.label: Fine silt

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Two bones from Dikika in Ethiopia show how hard the second question can be. In 2010 Shannon McPherron, Zeresenay Alemseged and colleagues reported marks on two animal bones 3.39 million years old that they read as cuts and scrapes from stone tools, which would put butchery 800,000 years before the earliest known tools.

shots.caption: Selam, the Dikika child, about 3.3 million years old, National Museum of Ethiopia

cues.speaker: research
cues.text: Manuel Domínguez-Rodrigo, Travis Pickering and Henry Bunn answered the same year that the marks matched damage from bones trampled in abrasive sand, and that no tools had been found. McPherron’s team replied that the shape, position and internal features of the marks matched experimental cuts rather than trampling. Statistical methods that separate cut marks from trampling have improved since, but two bones are a small sample, and the question is still open.

shots.question: Were the Dikika bones butchered 3.39 million years ago?

views.label: Cut marks
views.text: McPherron, Alemseged and colleagues, 2010: the shape, position and internal features of the marks match stone-tool cuts and percussion, not trampling.

views.label: Trampling
views.text: Domínguez-Rodrigo, Pickering and Bunn, 2010: the marks match experimental damage from bones trampled in abrasive sand, and no tools were found.

shots.status: Still open. Methods that separate cut marks from trampling statistically have improved, but two bones are a small sample.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The discipline that studies what happens to bones and stones after they are dropped, from trampling and gnawing to river transport and the collapse of cave floors, is called taphonomy, and it will sit behind many of the arguments in this series: whether the dead of Homo naledi were buried or washed in; whether a site in California holds mastodon bones broken by people 130,000 years ago; whether the sand at Madjedbebe kept its artefacts in place for 65,000 years.

shots.caption: Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, where rivers, lakes and volcanic ash sorted bones and stones for two million years

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Context is why archaeologists dig slowly, record every find in three dimensions, and are wary of objects picked up from the surface. When you hear that a find was excavated in place, or that it was a surface find, you now know why the words matter.

shots.caption: A section drawing: the record of what lay above what

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: How can anyone know that a spear is 200,000 years old, or a stone tool 3.3 million? Most of the dates in this series come from physics: from clocks that started ticking when an ash fell, a grain of sand was buried, or a plant died.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The most familiar clock is radiocarbon. Cosmic rays make a radioactive form of carbon in the upper air, and every living thing takes it up. When it dies, the intake stops and the carbon-14 decays, halving every 5,730 years. Willard Libby published the first dates in 1949 and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960. After about 50,000 years too little carbon-14 remains to measure, so radiocarbon covers only the last hundredth of the story. Raw ages also have to be calibrated against tree rings, cave deposits and lake sediments, because the amount of carbon-14 in the air has varied; the international calibration curve was last revised in 2020 and reaches back 55,000 years.

card.label: The half-life of carbon-14. After about 50,000 years too little is left to measure.
card.note: Libby, 1949; IntCal20 calibration curve, Reimer and colleagues, 2020

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Older sites need older clocks. Volcanic ash and lava contain potassium, which decays into argon gas at a known rate; the heat of an eruption drives out the old argon and resets the clock. In 1961 Jack Evernden and Garniss Curtis dated the ash beneath the skull that Mary Leakey had found at Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania to 1.75 million years, far older than almost anyone expected, and the human story suddenly grew. East Africa’s Rift Valley is layered with ash, which is why it provides the backbone of dates for early human fossils.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Earth’s magnetic field has flipped many times. Magnetic minerals in cooling lava or settling mud record the direction of the field, and the last full reversal, about 773,000 years ago, is a marker recognisable in sediments worldwide. A layer magnetised the wrong way round must be older than that.

card.label: The last full reversal of Earth’s magnetic field, a marker found in sediments worldwide

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Other clocks count damage. Natural radiation traps electrons in the crystals of quartz and feldspar; sunlight or heat empties the traps. Luminescence dating measures how much has built up since a grain of sand last saw daylight, or a flint was last burnt. Electron spin resonance does the same for tooth enamel. Uranium dissolved in cave water is built into stalagmites and crusts, and its decay into thorium dates them back to about half a million years. And cosmic rays make rare isotopes in quartz at the surface, which decay at different rates once a rock is washed deep into a cave: that is how the skeleton called Little Foot at Sterkfontein in South Africa was dated to about 3.67 million years by Darryl Granger and colleagues in 2015.

cues.speaker: research
cues.text: The Little Foot date shows how dating arguments run. Jan Kramers and Paul Dirks argued in 2017 that the quartz grains could have been washed in long before the skeleton, and that flowstones in the cave point to an age nearer 2.2 million years. Granger’s team answered that the flowstones had formed in later cavities and could not date the bones. In 2024 Francis Thackeray compared the fossil primates of the deposit with dated sequences elsewhere and arrived at about 3.6 million years, though earlier comparisons of the same kind had suggested between 2 and 2.6 million. Most researchers now accept an age near 3.7 million, with the caveat that a single site dated by one main method invites doubt.

card.question: How old is Little Foot?

views.label: About 3.67 million years
views.text: Granger and colleagues (2015, 2022): cosmogenic isotopes in quartz grains buried with the skeleton, on an isochron that corrects for reworked grains.

views.label: Nearer 2.2 million years
views.text: Kramers and Dirks (2017): the grains may predate the skeleton, and flowstones in the chamber give younger ages.

card.status: Thackeray (2024) reached about 3.6 million years from the fossil primates; the older age is the majority view, but it rests mainly on one method at one site.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: No method is perfect, so a well-dated site is dated by several, and this series gives dates as ranges, naming the method where it matters.

card.title: Which clock for which age
items: Radiocarbon: to about 50,000 years
Luminescence and electron spin resonance: to a few hundred thousand years, sometimes more
Uranium-thorium: to about 500,000 years in cave calcite
Argon and palaeomagnetism: hundreds of thousands to millions of years
Cosmogenic burial: about 200,000 to 5 million years

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Sometimes a single date can move a whole debate. In 2018 Dirk Hoffmann, Alistair Pike and colleagues reported uranium-thorium dates on thin calcite crusts that had grown over red paintings in three Spanish caves: La Pasiega, Maltravieso and Ardales. The crusts were at least 64,800 years old. Modern humans reached Spain more than 20,000 years later, so if the dates hold, the painters were Neanderthals.

cues.speaker: research
cues.text: The team argued that calcite can only grow after the paint beneath it is in place, so its age is a minimum age for the art, and that they had sampled many crusts, at three caves, with consistent results.

card.question: Did Neanderthals paint Spanish caves 65,000 years ago?

views.label: Yes: the crusts are minimum ages
views.text: Hoffmann, Pike and colleagues (2018): uranium-thorium dates on calcite over the paint at three caves, consistent and older than any modern human presence in Spain.

views.label: The dates may be too old
views.text: White and 43 colleagues (2020), Pons-Branchu and colleagues (2020): flowing water leaches uranium and inflates ages; some samples were beside the pigment; no other Neanderthal painting is known.

card.status: Published and contested. No independent method has confirmed or refuted the dates, and the authors stand by them.

cues.speaker: research
cues.text: In 2020 a group of 44 researchers led by Randall White answered that water flowing over cave walls can leach uranium out of calcite, making it appear older than it is, that some crusts sampled lay beside rather than over the pigment, and that no other Neanderthal site in Europe shows painting. Edwige Pons-Branchu and colleagues showed at Nerja Cave, also in Spain, that the same method can give ages far too old for layers of known age. Hoffmann and Pike replied that they had tested for uranium loss and found none where it mattered, and stood by their dates.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Where does it stand? The dates remain published and contested, and no independent method has yet confirmed or refuted them. Meanwhile uranium-series dating of a hand stencil on Muna Island and a painted hunting scene in Sulawesi, both in Indonesia, gave ages of at least 67,800 and 51,200 years, with the same method and similar questions about calcite. We will return to all of these caves. The point for now is that a date is an argument until other methods and other sites agree.

sources.cite: Hoffmann, D. L. et al. (2018). U-Th dating of carbonate crusts reveals Neandertal origin of Iberian cave art. Science 359, 912–915.
White, R. et al. (2020). Still no archaeological evidence that Neanderthals created Iberian cave art. Journal of Human Evolution 144, 102640.
Pons-Branchu, E. et al. (2020). U-series dating at Nerja cave reveal open system. Implications for the Neanderthal origin of cave art. Journal of Archaeological Science 117, 105120.
Hoffmann, D. L. et al. (2020). Response to White et al.’s reply: ‘Still no archaeological evidence that Neanderthals created Iberian cave art’. Journal of Human Evolution 144, 102810.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Bones and stones are not the only archive. Since the 1990s, molecules have become a second one. In 1997 Svante Pääbo’s laboratory in Munich recovered mitochondrial DNA from the Neanderthal fossil found in 1856 in the Neander valley. In 2010 his team in Leipzig published a draft Neanderthal genome, and the same year identified a wholly new human group, the Denisovans, from the DNA of a finger bone found in a Siberian cave. Pääbo received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2022.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: DNA breaks into ever shorter fragments and survives best in cold, dry places and in the dense petrous bone of the inner ear. The oldest human DNA sequenced so far comes from the Sima de los Huesos in Spain, about 430,000 years old. Beyond people, a mammoth tooth from Siberian permafrost yielded DNA more than a million years old in 2021, and in 2022 Eske Willerslev’s team read the DNA of an entire ecosystem, mastodons, reindeer and birch, from two-million-year-old sediment at Kap København in northern Greenland.

card.label: The oldest DNA yet read, from frozen sediment in northern Greenland
card.note: Kjær and colleagues, Nature, 2022. Oldest human DNA: Sima de los Huesos, about 430,000 years

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: DNA no longer needs a bone. In 2017 Viviane Slon and colleagues extracted Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA from the dirt of cave floors, and sediment DNA has since revealed who lived in caves that never yielded a fossil.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Proteins last longer than DNA. In 2020 enamel proteins placed Homo antecessor, about 800,000 years old, on the family tree. In 2025 Palesa Madupe and colleagues read enamel proteins from four Paranthropus teeth about two million years old at Swartkrans in South Africa and told which were male and which female, and Daniel Green’s team recovered protein fragments up to 18 million years old from fossil mammals of the Turkana Basin.

card.label: The oldest hominin proteins: four Paranthropus teeth from Swartkrans
card.note: Madupe and colleagues, Science, 2025. Mammal enamel proteins reach 18 million years (Green and colleagues, Nature, 2025)

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: In June 2025 proteins and a scrap of mitochondrial DNA from dental plaque tied the almost complete Harbin skull from northeast China, at least 146,000 years old, to the Denisovans, and proteins identified a jaw dredged from the seabed off Taiwan as a Denisovan man. A group known for fifteen years almost only from its genes had been given a face.

cues.speaker: research
cues.text: How far can molecules reach? Researchers in palaeoproteomics expect enamel proteins to help sort out relationships among hominins that will never yield DNA. Others caution that enamel preserves only a handful of proteins, so each fragment carries few informative differences; that contamination and chemical damage are hard to rule out; and that hominin DNA has not been recovered from anything older than about 430,000 years, with warm climates destroying it far faster.

card.question: How far back can molecules take us?

views.label: A deep molecular record
views.text: Enamel proteins now reach 2 million years for hominins and 18 million for other mammals; proteomics may sort out early hominin relationships that anatomy cannot.

views.label: A thin signal
views.text: Few proteins survive in enamel, each with few informative differences; contamination and damage are hard to exclude; DNA stops at about 430,000 years for humans.

card.status: Proteins reliably give sex and broad relationships for some species older than 2 million years; detailed family trees still rest mainly on anatomy.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Chemistry also tells us what people ate and where they grew up. Carbon isotopes in tooth enamel separate diets of leaves and fruit from diets of grasses and sedges; nitrogen tracks meat; strontium matches a tooth to the geology of the place where its owner spent childhood, and so reveals who moved.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The people in this story lived through climates that swung wildly. We know because the ocean floor and the ice remember. Tiny shelled creatures called foraminifera build their shells from seawater, and the ratio of oxygen isotopes in those shells tracks how much water was locked up in ice. In 2005 Lorraine Lisiecki and Maureen Raymo stacked 57 deep-sea records into a single curve covering 5.3 million years. Its numbered warm and cold stages, odd for warm, even for cold, are the calendar of the ice ages, and the sea-level curve along the bottom of this screen is built from records like it.

card.kicker: The calendar of the ice ages
card.title: Marine isotope stages
items: Odd numbers: warm stages. Stage 1 is the Holocene, stage 5e the last interglacial about 125,000 years ago
Even numbers: cold stages. Stage 2 holds the Last Glacial Maximum
The LR04 stack of Lisiecki and Raymo (2005) covers 5.3 million years

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Antarctic ice holds a more direct record: bubbles of ancient air. A European project at Dome C recovered 800,000 years of carbon dioxide and temperature. In January 2025 its successor, Beyond EPICA, reached bedrock at nearby Little Dome C with a core 2,800 metres long whose ice is more than 1.2 million years old. The last samples reached European laboratories in April 2026, and the analysis is under way.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: That core targets a puzzle. Between about 1.25 million and 700,000 years ago the rhythm of the ice ages changed: cycles of roughly 41,000 years, set by the tilt of Earth’s axis, gave way to longer and deeper cycles of about 100,000 years. The change is called the Mid-Pleistocene Transition, and nobody yet agrees why it happened. Proposals include the slow scouring of loose sediment from beneath the northern ice sheets, which let them grow thicker and more stable, and a long-term decline in carbon dioxide. Hominins had already lived in Europe and Asia for a million years when it began.

card.title: Orbital rhythms
items: Tilt of the axis: about 41,000 years
Wobble of the axis: about 21,000 years, which drives the monsoons
Shape of the orbit: about 100,000 years
After the Mid-Pleistocene Transition the 100,000-year beat dominates

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: In Africa the swings showed less as ice than as rain. The strength of the monsoon follows the wobble of Earth’s axis, about every 21,000 years, turning the Sahara green and then to desert again and again. Lake cores, stalagmites, pollen and fossil soils fill in the local detail. The climate archives give the Stone Age its weather; the sites give it its people.

sources.cite: Lisiecki, L. E. & Raymo, M. E. (2005). A Pliocene–Pleistocene stack of 57 globally distributed benthic δ18O records. Paleoceanography 20, PA1003.
EPICA community members (2004). Eight glacial cycles from an Antarctic ice core. Nature 429, 623–628.
Beyond EPICA – Oldest Ice (2025). Press release, 9 January 2025: Ice core more than 1.2 million years old drilled at Little Dome C. beyondepica.eu.
Clark, P. U. et al. (2006). The middle Pleistocene transition: characteristics, mechanisms, and implications for long-term changes in atmospheric pCO2. Quaternary Science Reviews 25, 3150–3184.

scenes.title: The world at the ice maximum

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Twenty thousand years ago, at the Last Glacial Maximum, you could have walked from England to Denmark, from Siberia to Alaska, and from New Guinea to Tasmania. Ice sheets up to three kilometres thick covered most of Canada and Scandinavia. So much water was locked up in them that the sea stood about 120 to 130 metres lower than today. Watch the coastlines on this globe as the timeline moves: the shelves that appear were dry land, and people lived on them.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: A 2020 study led by Jessica Tierney estimated that the world was about six degrees colder than before industrial times, with carbon dioxide near 190 parts per million, against more than 420 today. It was drier and dustier; tropical forests shrank and deserts grew.

card.label: Global mean temperature at the Last Glacial Maximum, compared with pre-industrial times
card.note: Tierney and colleagues, Nature, 2020. Sea level about 120 to 130 metres lower (Lambeck and colleagues, 2014)

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The drowned lowlands have names we gave them afterwards. Beringia joined Siberia to Alaska. Sundaland joined Sumatra, Java and Borneo to the Asian mainland, a lowland of more than a million square kilometres. Sahul united Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania. Doggerland joined Britain to the continent, and the floor of the Persian Gulf was a river valley.

card.title: The drowned lowlands
items: Beringia: Siberia to Alaska, cut by about 11,000 years ago
Sundaland: mainland Asia to Borneo and Java, largely drowned by 7,000 years ago
Sahul: Australia with New Guinea and Tasmania
Doggerland: Britain to the continent, gone by about 7,500 years ago

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Every one of those lands is now sea floor, and the archaeology of the people who lived on them is mostly lost, or reachable only by dredging and seismic survey. That loss shapes everything we think we know about coastlines and boats, and it will come up on every continent in this series.

sources.cite: Lambeck, K. et al. (2014). Sea level and global ice volumes from the Last Glacial Maximum to the Holocene. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 111, 15296–15303.
Tierney, J. E. et al. (2020). Glacial cooling and climate sensitivity revisited. Nature 584, 569–573.
Clark, P. U. et al. (2009). The Last Glacial Maximum. Science 325, 710–714.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Then the ice began to melt, but not smoothly. Deglaciation was paced by changes in Earth’s orbit that increased northern summer sunshine from about 20,000 years ago, amplified by rising carbon dioxide. The path was jagged because meltwater disturbed the Atlantic circulation that carries heat north.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: About 14,700 years ago the circulation strengthened and Greenland warmed by around ten degrees within decades. The sea surged: corals drilled off Tahiti record a rise of some 14 to 18 metres in about three and a half centuries, four centimetres a year.

card.label: The warming over Greenland at the start of the Bølling interstadial, about 14,700 years ago
card.note: Meltwater Pulse 1A: about 14 to 18 metres of sea-level rise in about 350 years (Deschamps and colleagues, 2012)

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Around 12,900 years ago the North Atlantic world plunged back into near-glacial cold for twelve centuries, a relapse called the Younger Dryas after an Arctic flower whose remains reappear in Scandinavian lake mud. When it ended, 11,700 years ago, the Holocene began, the epoch in which every farming society has lived. Its start is formally defined in a Greenland ice core, at a depth of 1,492 metres, where a team led by Jørgen Peder Steffensen showed that the change took only a few years.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The rising water drowned whole landscapes. Around 8,150 years ago a vast undersea landslide off Norway, the Storegga slide, sent a tsunami across the North Sea that left sand several metres above the shorelines of the time; Vince Gaffney’s team has argued that it struck a Doggerland already breaking into islands. Sundaland went under; Tasmania and then New Guinea became islands. Patrick Nunn and Nicholas Reid have argued that some Aboriginal Australian stories preserve memories of coastlines lost more than 7,000 years ago; sceptics reply that people can infer past landscapes from what they see today, and that dating a story is hard.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Meanwhile the Sahara turned green, with lakes, hippos and grasslands. People everywhere adapted: fishing, gathering seeds and nuts, and staying longer in one place. The great thaw is the stage on which farming, villages and metal will appear in later episodes.

sources.cite: Deschamps, P. et al. (2012). Ice-sheet collapse and sea-level rise at the Bølling warming 14,600 years ago. Nature 483, 559–564.
Steffensen, J. P. et al. (2008). High-resolution Greenland ice core data show abrupt climate change happens in few years. Science 321, 680–684.
Walker, M. et al. (2009). Formal definition and dating of the GSSP for the base of the Holocene using the Greenland NorthGRIP ice core. Journal of Quaternary Science 24, 3–17.
Gaffney, V. et al. (2020). Multi-proxy characterisation of the Storegga tsunami and its impact on the early Holocene landscapes of the southern North Sea. Geosciences 10, 270.
Nunn, P. D. & Reid, N. J. (2016). Aboriginal memories of inundation of the Australian coast dating from more than 7000 years ago. Australian Geographer 47, 11–47.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: What caused the Younger Dryas? The question has produced one of the longest arguments in Quaternary science, and one that has crossed into popular culture. Here are the positions.

cues.speaker: research
cues.text: The most widely held explanation goes back to Wallace Broecker in 1989. As the Laurentide ice sheet retreated, meltwater pooled in glacial Lake Agassiz, larger than any lake today, and a sudden outflow to the ocean freshened the North Atlantic and weakened the circulation that warms Europe. For decades the flood path was elusive; Broecker himself wrote in 2006 that the failure to find it was disconcerting. In 2010 Julian Murton and colleagues identified gravels and an eroded surface along the Mackenzie River, pointing to a drainage north into the Arctic Ocean, and in 2018 Lloyd Keigwin’s team found the freshening recorded in sediment cores off the Mackenzie delta. Whether that water alone could cool the region for twelve centuries is still debated; a weakened circulation sustained by further freshwater is a common answer.

cues.speaker: research
cues.text: A rival explanation was proposed in 2007 by Richard Firestone, James Kennett and colleagues: that fragments of a comet exploded over or struck North America about 12,900 years ago, igniting wildfires, destabilising the ice sheet, and contributing to the extinction of the mammoths and the end of the Clovis culture. Its proponents, organised as the Comet Research Group, point to a layer they call the Younger Dryas boundary: magnetic microspherules, nanodiamonds, melted glass and a platinum spike found at many sites, including a platinum peak in Greenland ice reported by Michail Petaev in 2013, and meltglass at the village of Abu Hureyra in Syria described by Andrew Moore in 2020. Martin Sweatman’s 2021 review concluded that the evidence had been replicated widely enough to be taken seriously.

card.question: What caused the Younger Dryas?

views.label: Meltwater
views.text: Broecker (1989), Murton and colleagues (2010), Keigwin and colleagues (2018): Lake Agassiz drained north through the Mackenzie valley, freshened the Arctic and North Atlantic and weakened the ocean circulation. The majority view.

views.label: A cosmic impact
views.text: Firestone, Kennett and colleagues (2007); Petaev (2013); Moore (2020); Sweatman (2021): microspherules, nanodiamonds, meltglass and platinum at a boundary layer on several continents mark a comet airburst.

views.label: The critics
views.text: Meltzer and colleagues (2014): the layers are not securely dated. Holliday and 12 colleagues (2023): the markers are not unique to impacts, no crater exists, and the extinctions and Clovis show no sudden break.

card.status: Most Quaternary scientists favour meltwater and regard the impact as unproven; its proponents regard it as prematurely dismissed. Three of the group’s papers were retracted in 2025 and 2026.

cues.speaker: research
cues.text: Critics answer on several fronts. Independent teams failed to find nanodiamonds or spherules at the same levels, or found them at many other levels too. A 2014 study led by David Meltzer argued that most of the claimed boundary layers were not securely dated to 12,900 years. No crater of the right age is known: the Hiawatha crater under the Greenland ice, once a candidate, was dated in 2022 to 58 million years. And the mammoths and the Clovis culture show no sudden break. In 2023 Vance Holliday and twelve co-authors published a long review in Earth-Science Reviews under the title of a comprehensive refutation. Proponents replied in 2024 that the review misrepresented their studies, and Holliday’s group rebutted in turn.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The argument has since moved into the record of retractions. In 2025 Scientific Reports retracted a Comet Research Group paper claiming that an airburst destroyed the Bronze Age city of Tall el-Hammam in Jordan, citing problems with its data. In February 2026 the journal PLOS One retracted two 2025 papers by group members, one on shocked quartz in North America and one on sediment cores from Baffin Bay, citing incomplete sampling, an age model that mixed dates from centuries on either side of the boundary, and, in the Baffin Bay case, particles presented as cosmic spherules that were the shells of single-celled marine organisms. The group disputes the retractions and continues to publish, partly in a journal of its own.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Where does the field stand? Most Quaternary scientists regard the meltwater explanation as the best supported, and the impact hypothesis as unproven. Its proponents regard it as prematurely dismissed. The lost-civilisation reading of the same event, popularised by Graham Hancock, is a further step, which we will examine alongside Göbekli Tepe in episode 5. In this series each claim is weighed by its evidence, and the evidence is what you have just heard.

card.title: The Younger Dryas
items: Meltwater from Lake Agassiz: the majority explanation, with a flood path identified in 2010 and 2018
Cosmic impact: published since 2007, replicated by its proponents, disputed by independent teams, three papers retracted in 2025 and 2026
No crater of the right age is known

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Some of the most dramatic stories about our past come from single studies. Three examples show how the field tests them.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: In 2023 Wangjie Hu, Haipeng Li and colleagues published a method called FitCoal, which reads past population size from the pattern of genetic variants in living people. Applied to more than 3,000 modern genomes, it indicated that between about 930,000 and 813,000 years ago the ancestors of modern humans fell to about 1,280 breeding individuals and stayed there for more than 100,000 years.

card.label: Breeding individuals in the claimed bottleneck of 930,000 to 813,000 years ago

cues.speaker: research
cues.text: Other population geneticists could not reproduce the result. In 2025 Yun Deng, Rasmus Nielsen and Yun Song argued that the bottleneck was likely a statistical artefact, and Trevor Cousins and Arun Durvasula concluded that the evidence was insufficient: established methods applied to the same genomes show nothing, a model without any bottleneck fits the data better, a population split into groups that exchanged migrants can mimic a crash, and the signal fails to appear in people outside Africa, who should carry it too. Hu and Li’s group replied in 2026 with simulations in which their method recovered sharp bottlenecks that the competing method smoothed away. The question is open; most specialists currently doubt the crash.

card.question: Did our ancestors nearly die out 900,000 years ago?

views.label: A severe bottleneck
views.text: Hu, Li and colleagues (2023, 2026): FitCoal finds a drop to about 1,280 breeding individuals lasting more than 100,000 years, and recovers such events in simulations.

views.label: A statistical artefact
views.text: Deng, Nielsen and Song (2025), Cousins and Durvasula (2025): other methods see nothing, a model without a bottleneck fits better, population structure can mimic a crash, and non-Africans lack the signal.

card.status: Unresolved; most population geneticists doubt the bottleneck. Ancient proteins from fossils of that age may eventually help.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: About 74,000 years ago the Toba volcano in northern Sumatra erupted, one of the largest eruptions of the past two million years, and its ash fell across India. In 1998 Stanley Ambrose proposed that a volcanic winter reduced our ancestors to a few thousand adults. Archaeologists went looking. At Jwalapuram in India, Michael Petraglia’s team found the same kinds of tools below and above the ash. At Pinnacle Point in South Africa, almost 9,000 kilometres away, Eugene Smith and Curtis Marean identified microscopic shards of Toba glass in layers where occupation continued without a break. In Ethiopia, John Kappelman’s team found in 2024 that people at Shinfa-Metema adapted to longer dry seasons by fishing in shrinking pools. Genomes show no crash at that date. Toba is now widely seen as a regional disaster, not a near-extinction.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: About 41,000 years ago Earth’s magnetic field weakened to a fraction of its strength and its poles wandered, an event named after lava flows at Laschamps in France. In 2021 Alan Cooper, Chris Turney and colleagues dated it precisely with radiocarbon from a kauri tree preserved in a New Zealand swamp, called the crisis the Adams Event, and linked it to megafaunal extinctions in Australia, the end of the Neanderthals and a rise in cave art. Andrea Picin, John Hawks and others replied that most of those events were already under way thousands of years earlier, and that ice cores show no marked climate change at the time. In 2025 Agnit Mukhopadhyay and colleagues modelled how auroras and radiation would have reached lower latitudes, and speculated that clothing, ochre and caves gave Homo sapiens an edge over Neanderthals. The idea is untested.

card.question: Did the magnetic excursion of 41,000 years ago change human history?

views.label: A global crisis
views.text: Cooper, Turney and colleagues (2021): ozone loss and climate shifts contributed to extinctions, Neanderthal decline and new behaviours; Mukhopadhyay and colleagues (2025) add a possible advantage for clothed, ochre-using Homo sapiens.

views.label: Coincidence
views.text: Picin, Hawks and others (2021): the extinctions and the Neanderthal decline began earlier, and ice cores and cave records show no distinct climate event at the time.

card.status: Most researchers remain unconvinced of major effects on people. Precise dating of sites against the radiocarbon record of the excursion is the test.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The pattern across all three is the same: a striking claim, a search for the evidence that would have to exist if it were true, and a field that moves slowly toward an answer. It is how every argument in this series will be handled.

scenes.title: The whole story in one sweep

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Before the continents get their own episodes, here is the whole story in one sweep. Seven million years ago, in Africa, an ape began to walk upright. Sahelanthropus from Chad, Orrorin from Kenya and Ardipithecus from Ethiopia are the candidates for the earliest members of our lineage, and each is argued over.

card.title: Upright apes
items: Sahelanthropus, Chad, about 7 million years
Orrorin, Kenya, about 6 million years
Ardipithecus, Ethiopia, 4.4 million years

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: By 3.5 million years ago the australopiths, Lucy’s kind, walked the East African rift and the caves of South Africa, and someone at Lomekwi was breaking stone. By 2.8 million years ago the first fossils placed in our own genus, Homo, appear in Ethiopia. By 2 million years ago Homo erectus, tall, long-legged and larger-brained, had appeared; soon it was making handaxes, and hominins had begun to leave Africa.

card.title: Australopiths and the first Homo
items: Lucy, Hadar, 3.2 million years
Laetoli footprints, 3.66 million years
Oldest Homo jaw, Ledi-Geraru, 2.8 million years
Handaxes by 1.76 million years

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Stone tools 2.1 million years old at Shangchen in China and fossils 1.8 million years old at Dmanisi in Georgia mark that first great expansion. Its descendants reached Java, Flores and Luzon, where island dwarfs evolved, and Europe, where by 400,000 years ago hominins hunted with wooden spears and tended fire.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: From about 430,000 years ago the human family branched. Neanderthals held Europe and western Asia; Denisovans, known first from DNA, ranged from Siberia to Tibet and Taiwan; Homo naledi, small-brained and long-armed, left its dead deep in a South African cave, buried deliberately, its discoverers argue. In Africa our own species took shape, with fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco about 315,000 years old, and with beads, ochre and engraved lines appearing over the following 200,000 years.

card.title: Many ways of being human
items: Neanderthals: Europe and western Asia
Denisovans: Siberia to Tibet and Taiwan
Homo naledi: South Africa, 335,000 to 236,000 years
Homo sapiens: Jebel Irhoud, about 315,000 years

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Homo sapiens left Africa more than once. The dispersal that mattered most began about 70,000 years ago, crossed Arabia and southern Asia, and reached Australia by 50,000 years ago, or 65,000 by a contested date, and Europe by 45,000. Neanderthals and Denisovans mixed with the newcomers, and then vanished, leaving their DNA in most people alive today.

card.label: Neanderthal DNA in people outside Africa; Denisovan DNA reaches several percent in New Guinea and Australia
card.note: Green and colleagues, 2010; Reich and colleagues, 2010

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: In the depths of the last ice age people painted caves, carved ivory, domesticated the dog, and crossed from Siberia into the Americas, by 21,000 years ago if the White Sands footprints are as old as their dates say. As the ice melted, people in at least seven regions began to farm, independently: the Levant, China, New Guinea, Mesoamerica, the Andes, eastern North America and the African Sahel.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Villages became towns. Göbekli Tepe’s pillars rose in Anatolia about 11,500 years ago, before pottery and before wheat was fully domesticated. Copper was smelted in the Balkans by 7,000 years ago, and bronze came into everyday use in Mesopotamia about 5,000 years ago. The last voyages of the Stone Age settled the Pacific: Lapita canoes reached Fiji and Tonga about 2,800 years ago, and their descendants reached New Zealand only about 700 years ago, when Europe was building cathedrals.

card.title: Towns, metal and the last voyages
items: Göbekli Tepe, about 11,500 years ago
Copper smelting in the Balkans, about 7,000 years ago
Bronze common in Mesopotamia, about 5,000 years ago
Lapita in Fiji and Tonga, about 2,800 years ago; New Zealand, about 700

cues.speaker: narrator

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: A word this series uses constantly needs a definition. A hominin is a human or any extinct relative more closely related to us than to chimpanzees and bonobos. The word says nothing about brains, tools or speech; it is about a branch of the family tree.

card.title: Hominin
items: Humans and all extinct relatives closer to us than to chimpanzees and bonobos
Includes australopiths, Paranthropus, Homo erectus, Neanderthals, Denisovans and us
Says nothing about intelligence or tools

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Species names are working hypotheses. Two researchers looking at the same jaw may place it in different species, and the record is thin: the whole story of the first three million years rests on a few thousand fragments. This series will name arguments as arguments and say who holds each view. Where genetics has changed the picture, as it has for the Neanderthals, the Denisovans and our own origins, it will say how.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The hunched, grunting caveman of cartoons is a nineteenth-century invention. Lubbock, who coined Palaeolithic, explained ancient Europeans through comparison with what he called modern savages. Between 1911 and 1913 Marcellin Boule reconstructed the Neanderthal skeleton from La Chapelle-aux-Saints in France as a stooped, bent-kneed brute. In 1957 William Straus and Alexander Cave showed that the man had severe arthritis, and that Neanderthals stood as upright as we do.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The same thinking justified colonial rule. Aboriginal Australians, Tasmanians, the San and others were labelled Stone Age peoples or living fossils, as if they had no history. In fact, living foragers such as the Hadza of Tanzania and the San of the Kalahari have long histories of change, trade and contact with farmers and states, as the Kalahari debate opened by Edwin Wilmsen in 1989 made clear. They are contemporary peoples. The Stone Age is a label for tools, not for the worth of the people who used them.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The people of the Stone Age crossed seas, painted caves, made music, cared for the sick and injured, and shaped whole landscapes with fire. Their descendants include everyone alive today.

Wilmsen, E. N. (1989). Land Filled with Flies: A Political Economy of the Kalahari. University of Chicago Press.
Wood, B. & Harrison, T. (2011). The evolutionary context of the first hominins. Nature 470, 347–352.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: The Stone Age has no single end. In this series it ends, region by region, when metal came into everyday use. Southwest Asia and southeast Europe went first: smelted copper by about 7,000 years ago at Belovode in Serbia, bronze common in Mesopotamia by about 5,000. China used bronze on a large scale from about 4,000 years ago. Much of sub-Saharan Africa went from stone straight to iron within the last 3,000 years, with no Bronze Age at all. In the Americas, people hammered native copper around the Great Lakes for thousands of years and Andean societies later smelted gold, silver and copper, but stone remained the everyday material. Australia and most Pacific islands used no metal before European contact.

card.title: A patchwork ending
items: Balkans and Iran: smelted copper by about 7,000 years ago
Mesopotamia and the Aegean: bronze common by about 5,000 years ago
China: bronze on a large scale from about 4,000 years ago
Sub-Saharan Africa: stone to iron, mostly in the last 3,000 years
Australia and the Pacific: no metal before European contact

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Stone stayed useful long after. Flint sickles remained common in the Bronze Age. In highland New Guinea, ground stone axes were quarried and traded into the twentieth century. An obsidian blade has an edge finer than a surgical scalpel, and some surgeons have used them. When this series says the Stone Age ended, it means only that a new material had arrived. The skills did not leave.

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Big questions remain open, and this series will follow them. When did people first reach the Americas: 23,000 years ago, as the White Sands footprints suggest, with three kinds of radiocarbon dates now agreeing, or after 16,000, as most sites indicate? When did they reach Australia: 65,000 years ago, if the sand at Madjedbebe holds its artefacts in place, or about 50,000, as genetics and most other sites suggest? Who made the first tools, and was Lomekwi one of their sites? What did the Denisovans look like, now that one skull has a name? Did Homo naledi bury its dead? Why did our species alone survive? Did farming begin in one place and spread, or in many? And how did inequality begin?

card.title: What the series will follow
items: First people in the Americas: 23,000 years ago, or after 16,000?
First Australians: 65,000 or 50,000 years ago?
Who made the first tools?
What did the Denisovans look like?
Did Homo naledi bury its dead?
Why did only our species survive?
How did farming, and inequality, begin?

cues.speaker: narrator
cues.text: Alongside these, the series will weigh views that most specialists reject but that have published proponents and a large public: the comet that ended the ice age; Göbekli Tepe as a record of the stars; a lost civilisation of the ice age; a pyramid older than the pyramids at Gunung Padang in Java; a Stone Age crossing of the Atlantic. Each will get the same treatment: the claim as its supporters put it, the evidence they cite, the answers of critics, and where the field stands, so that you can weigh it yourself.
